content:
According to the Financial Times, newly unsealed court documents show that OpenAI is disappointed with the adoption of ChatGPT through Apple Intelligence, stating that the service's performance since its 2024 launch has "fallen far short of expectations." Below are the details.

OpenAI is asking the court to rule before trial

In August 2025, Elon Musk announced that X, now folded into SpaceXAI, would sue Apple and OpenAI over alleged collusion to suppress AI competitors. The dispute stems from OpenAI's deal to integrate ChatGPT into Apple Intelligence and Siri.

Once the lawsuit was formally filed, the claims went beyond Musk's initial public complaints about App Store rankings. X and SpaceXAI also accused Apple of trying to stymie the development of "super apps," including X's plans to transform itself into an "everything app."

Over the following weeks and months, the various companies filed briefs, allegations, and rebuttals with the court. Apple and OpenAI both argued across multiple filings that their agreement was not the exclusive partnership the lawsuit alleged; the court documents also revealed some new details about the nature of that partnership.

Some of those details emerged in filings OpenAI submitted today. The Financial Times first reported that OpenAI "said it was disappointed by how little interest Apple Intelligence's ChatGPT-powered features for iPhone users generated after the 2024 deal."

The report continues:

Wednesday's court filings indicate that when the 2024 deal was struck, OpenAI expected a "halo effect" from Apple's promotion and brand association, and anticipated more subscriptions from Apple Intelligence users. But one month after the ChatGPT integration launched, performance "appeared off to a slow start," and OpenAI immediately lowered its projections for weekly active users. The filings continue that by summer 2025, "it had become clear that Apple's ChatGPT integration was performing far below expectations."

The report also notes that today's filings contain several redacted passages of dialogue, but the unredacted portions show that OpenAI executives feared Apple might "want to move faster" to find another AI partner.

When Apple Intelligence was first unveiled in 2024, senior vice president of software engineering Craig Federighi said in an interview that Apple ultimately wanted to let users choose between different AI models, explicitly mentioning Google Gemini as a possible future integration option.

Although that particular partnership did not materialise, Apple has since switched to using Google's Gemini model to help power the new Siri AI; at the same time, Xcode has expanded support for Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI coding agents.

Returning to today's filings, the Financial Times notes that the documents also blame one factor for the slow adoption: the way Apple integrated ChatGPT—the feature is off by default.

Finally, Reuters also mentions that OpenAI is arguing that SpaceX's recent securities filings undermine SpaceXAI's claims that the Apple partnership harms competition. In its filings, OpenAI points out that SpaceX's IPO registration statement is "replete with disclosures that are the opposite of the competitive harm alleged in the lawsuit."

On those grounds, OpenAI is asking Judge Mark Pittman to rule in its favour on SpaceXAI's antitrust claims before the case goes to trial. The case is currently scheduled for trial in January.
